name: ネパールステーション (Nepal Station)

claims.text: No information on dedicated fryers or separate prep areas for wheat-free dishes was found in any reviewed source. Cross-contamination risk is unknown and must be confirmed directly with staff.

Soy sauce is not a standard ingredient in Nepalese cooking; the cuisine relies on mustard oil, ghee, and spice blends rather than soy-based condiments. However, the restaurant also serves izakaya-style dishes which may use Japanese condiments containing wheat.
The kitchen handles meat, egg, and dairy alongside vegetable dishes. No separation protocol has been publicly documented. Ask staff whether vegetable curries are cooked in shared pans.

The manager speaks fluent Japanese and can discuss menu contents. Staff are Nepalese nationals; complex allergy queries in English or detailed Japanese may require advance notice by phone (052-202-8802).

Nepalese cuisine is inherently rice-centred (dal bhat, basmati rice) with many naturally vegetable- and legume-based dishes, offering more GF-friendly options than Indian-restaurant menus that rely on naan.
Tabelog lists a vegetarian menu (ベジタリアンメニューあり) and a health/wellness menu, indicating the kitchen is accustomed to accommodating plant-based diners.

name: 山本屋総本家 金シャチ横丁店 (Yamamotoya Souhonke Kinshachi Yokocho)

claims.text: Noodles are made entirely from wheat flour; wheat is inseparable from the dish. No gluten-free alternative exists.
Buckwheat (soba) flour is used as dusting powder on all udon noodles, creating an additional cross-contact risk for both gluten-sensitive and soba-allergic diners.

The miso tare contains soy sauce (shoyu), which contains wheat. Allergen labeling for Yamamotoya products explicitly lists wheat (小麦) as a declared allergen across noodles, miso blend, and broth components.
Broth is made from katsuobushi (bonito), mackerel, mackerel pike, and sardine. The miso blend contains bonito and mackerel. No plant-only broth option is available.

No information found about staff allergy handling procedures at the restaurant. Given the allergen complexity (wheat in noodles and broth, soba dusting powder, multiple fish), diners with serious allergies should contact the restaurant directly before visiting.
